extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. The dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages, sourced from the Book Corpus.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., & Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages that were relatively easy for standard language models were filtered out using a combination of four language models. Remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject guessed based on the whole passage; (3) if both correct, more subjects tried to guess based on the target sentence only (up to 10 unsuccessful guesses). Only passages where no subject could guess from the target sentence alone were included.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015) - a collection of unpublished novels.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list from the Book Corpus. Passages were then filtered using four language models (a pre-trained RNN, a 4-gram model, an RNN and feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus); any passage whose target word had probability ≥ 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded. Context size was set to the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdsourced annotation via CrowdFlower in three steps: (1) one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if correct, (2) a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if also correct, (3) more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, with 3 guesses per sentence, until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. Passages that passed all steps (guessable from full passage but not from target sentence alone) were included. The same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Strict perfect-match approach: required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word in the full passage condition, and no subject (out of up to 10) was able to provide it based on local context only (with 3 guesses each). In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 annotators in passage condition (both must guess correctly) and up to 10 annotators in target-sentence-only condition (none may guess correctly), with 3 guesses allowed per sentence in step 3.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: English speakers recruited via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used for filtering: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011), a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, is available at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set will be made available at the time of a planned public competition.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Target words in LAMBADA are heavily skewed toward proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and verbs (7.7%). Proper nouns are hugely over-represented compared to the POS distribution in the input. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. LAMBADA items contain quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% vs. 61%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA was constructed by filtering out passages where simple language models could predict the upcoming word, so standard language models are bound to fail on it by design. The strict perfect-match criterion excludes passages where broad-context subjects might provide plausible synonymous continuations. Financial/practical considerations precluded more subjects at stage 1 to improve filtering quality.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of computational models for text understanding, specifically language models' ability to take broad discourse context into account when predicting a word. The training data (203M words from 2,662 novels) can be used for training language models. The development set can be used to fine-tune models. The test set is intended as a challenging benchmark.
